---
title: "Metric Dependence in Seasonal Heat-Stress Timing"
description: "Heat metrics can move together hour-to-hour yet identify different periods as the hottest part of the year."
status: "Manuscript in preparation"
year: 2026
---

## Research question

When heat-action planning targets the hottest part of the year, do commonly used heat-stress metrics agree on **when** that period occurs?

## Approach

Using hourly ERA5 reanalysis for India from 1980–2024, we compute, for every grid cell and year, the contiguous 90-day period maximizing four metrics: 2 m air temperature, Wet-Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT), Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI), and Extended Heat Index (EHI), and compare their timing.

## Headline results

- The metrics track one another closely hour-to-hour, with Spearman correlations of about **0.84–0.97**.
- They nevertheless peak in sequence: **temperature → UTCI → EHI → WBGT**.
- Over the Indo-Gangetic Plain, WBGT- and temperature-defined 90-day windows differ by about **seven weeks in the median**.
- At roughly a fifth of grid cells, those windows fail to overlap at all in at least one year.
- Among the hottest decile of hours—the observations that determine the seasonal maximum—temperature and WBGT lose essentially all rank association in 2024 (**Kendall's τ = −0.06**).
- The share of years in which a metric selects the humid season rises through the metric sequence, reaching **0.47 for WBGT**.

## High correlation does not guarantee agreement in extremes

The central result is a scale paradox: the metrics look highly interchangeable over the bulk of the hourly distribution, yet the observations that determine the seasonal extreme are precisely where their ordering becomes much less stable.

### 1. The metrics are highly correlated at representative grid points

<figure class="research-figure research-figure-wide">
<a href="/assets/figures/wbgt-utci-spearman-representative.png" target="_blank"><img src="/assets/figures/wbgt-utci-spearman-representative.png" alt="Six representative pair plots showing strong pairwise rank correlations among air temperature, EHI, UTCI and WBGT."></a>
<figcaption><strong>Strong hourly correlation coexists with divergent extremes.</strong> Each panel uses a representative grid cell at the median long-run timing difference for that metric pair. The upper triangles report rank correlations, the diagonals show 2024 distributions, and the lower triangles show pairwise scatter with LOWESS fits. The central clouds are tight and close to linear, but the hot tails bend and fan apart. The full hourly archive gives pairwise Spearman correlations of roughly 0.84–0.97.</figcaption>
</figure>

### 2. Agreement deteriorates in the hottest 10% of hours

<figure class="research-figure research-figure-narrow">
<a href="/assets/figures/wbgt-utci-top10-discordance.png" target="_blank"><img src="/assets/figures/wbgt-utci-top10-discordance.png" alt="Maps of pairwise discordant-pair fractions for full-hourly data and for top-decile heat-stress hours."></a>
<figcaption><strong>The extreme tail is much more discordant.</strong> The left column shows pairwise discordant-pair fractions over the full hourly record; the top-decile columns show the same idea after restricting attention to the hottest part of the distribution. Discordance rises sharply across much of India. For temperature versus WBGT, the hottest-decile rank association is essentially absent in 2024 (Kendall's τ = −0.06).</figcaption>
</figure>

This is the key bridge between the first and third figures: a high correlation calculated over all hours is dominated by the large central part of the distribution. But the 90-day block maximum is selected by the **extreme tail**, where the metrics disagree much more.

### 3. That tail disagreement moves the 90-day maximum by weeks

<figure class="research-figure research-figure-narrow">
<a href="/assets/figures/wbgt-utci-blockmaxima-timing.webp" target="_blank"><img src="/assets/figures/wbgt-utci-blockmaxima-timing.webp" alt="Maps of pairwise differences in the timing of maximizing 90-day heat-stress windows across India, including 2024 differences, long-run medians and Sen-slope trends."></a>
<figcaption><strong>Pairwise disagreement in the timing of the hottest quarter is large and signed.</strong> Rows are the six metric pairs (U = UTCI, W = WBGT, T = air temperature, H = Extended Heat Index). Columns show the timing difference in 2024, the long-run median difference, and the Sen's-slope trend over 1980–2024. The sign follows the row label order: positive/red means the first metric peaks later. The 2024 and median colour scales saturate at ±40 days, so still larger differences—including non-overlap beyond 90 days—appear at the scale limits.</figcaption>
</figure>

The disagreement in the extreme tail is therefore not a small statistical curiosity. It is large enough to move the selected 90-day hottest period by **many tens of days** across broad regions. Over the Indo-Gangetic Plain, the median WBGT-versus-temperature difference is about seven weeks; in some grid-cell years the two 90-day windows do not overlap at all.

Together, the three figures show why an overall correlation coefficient is not sufficient for deciding whether heat-stress metrics are interchangeable for seasonal planning. **The relevant question is whether they preserve ordering in the extreme part of the distribution that selects the maximum window.**

## Metric choice as a normative choice

Different heat metrics encode different physical and physiological emphases: temperature, humidity, radiation, wind, or combinations of them. A warning calendar therefore does not simply *measure* a pre-existing hottest season; it operationalises a definition of heat stress and thereby determines whose exposures receive policy attention.

This is one example of the modelling approach I want to develop more broadly: identify where technical definitions carry normative consequences, then quantify how much those choices change the conclusion.

Figures, code, and manuscript links will continue to be added as the paper is finalized.
